title: Amide resonance
subtitle: The nitrogen lone pair is shared with the carbonyl

neutral-form.caption: acetamide
neutral-form.learnerPrompt: Draw the charge-separated resonance form of acetamide. Move only lone pairs and π bonds.
hintTiers: Which atom next to the carbonyl group has a lone pair?
Nitrogen's lone pair makes a C=N π bond. Carbon cannot have five bonds, so the C=O π bond moves onto oxygen. Two arrows.
Arrow 1: the nitrogen lone pair into the C–N bond. Arrow 2: the C=O π bond onto oxygen.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Resonance arrows never break or make σ bonds: the atoms stay exactly where they are. Move only lone pairs and π bonds.
The oxygen lone pair pushing in would give carbon five bonds, and there is no π bond on the other side for carbon to lose. Start from the nitrogen lone pair.
The π pair moves towards oxygen, the more electronegative atom, not onto carbon.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right idea: nitrogen's lone pair forms a C=N π bond. But carbon now has five bonds. Push the C=O π bond onto oxygen at the same time.

steps.explanationAfterStep: This form has more charges, so it contributes less than the neutral one, but it matters: rotation about the C–N bond is slow at room temperature, and the nitrogen lone pair is not free to act as a base. It also makes the amide carbonyl the least electrophilic of the acid derivatives.

mechanismSummary: The nitrogen lone pair forms a C=N π bond and the C=O π bond moves onto oxygen. The charge-separated form is a real contributor: the C–N bond has partial double-bond character, the amide is flat and nitrogen is barely basic.
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapter 7 (Delocalization and conjugation)
